# Spinal cord tracts and reflexes

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > Spinal cord tracts and reflexes*

[Original Article Link](/library/G60BmS)

---

## Summary

The spinal cord is part of the <u>central nervous system</u> and coordinates motor, sensory, and reflex signals. Anatomically, the spinal cord is located within the <u>spinal canal</u> and extends from the bottom of the medulla (at the first <u>cervical vertebra</u> C1) to the <u>conus medullaris</u> (between L1 and L2). Blood is supplied to the spinal cord from the branches of the <u>vertebral artery</u> and drains into the <u>vertebral</u> <u>veins</u>. Internally, the cord can be divided into <u>gray matter</u> centrally and <u>white matter</u> peripherally (unlike in the <u>brain</u>, where this division is inverted). The <u>gray matter</u> is composed of the <u>anterior horn</u>, which contains <u>the cell</u> bodies of motor <u>neurons</u>; the <u>dorsal horn</u>, which contains <u>the cell</u> bodies of sensory <u>neurons</u>; and the <u>lateral horn</u>, which contains <u>the cell</u> bodies of <u>preganglionic</u> <u>sympathetic</u> <u>neurons</u>. The <u>white matter</u> contains descending and ascending tracts. The descending tracts transmit motor signals to the periphery and the ascending tracts transmit sensory signals to the <u>brain</u>. Thirty-one pairs of peripheral <u>spinal nerves</u> arise segmentally from the spinal cord and conduct autonomic, motor, sensory, and reflex signals between the <u>CNS</u> and the body. Clinically relevant <u>spinal reflexes</u> include the <u>patellar reflex</u>, <u>ankle reflex</u>, <u>biceps reflex</u>, and <u>triceps reflex</u>. Each <u>spinal nerve</u> carries <u>dermatomes</u>, which are somatic sensory fibers that correspond with a specific and identifiable region of <u>skin</u>. Each <u>dermatome</u> is supplied by a single spinal cord level and is, therefore, useful in identifying specific levels of damage in <u>spinal cord injuries</u>. The development of the spinal cord begins around the third week of <u>gestation</u> during the process of <u>neurulation</u>. The spinal cord is derived from the <u>neural tube</u>. Conditions that affect the spinal cord include <u>spinal shock</u> (related to trauma), <u>central cord syndrome</u>, and <u>multiple sclerosis</u>.

## Gross anatomy

### Structures of the spinal cord




| Structure | Anatomy | Function | Characteristic features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| White matter | <br><br>* Bundles of the following nerve fibers:<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> funiculus<br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> funiculus<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> funiculus<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> median <u>fissure</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> median sulcus: separates the <u>posterior columns</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Contains bundles of myelinated <u>axons</u> called tracts or fasciculi<br><br>* <u>Axons</u> ascend or descend in the spinal cord within the <u>white matter</u> to transmit signals between the <u>CNS</u> and periphery.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Surrounds the <u>gray matter</u> peripherally<br><br>* White appearance due to <u>myelin</u><br><br>* Does not contain <u>dendrites</u><br><br><br> |
| Gray matter | <br><br>* <u>Anterior gray column</u> (<u>ventral horn</u>)<br><br>* <u>Posterior gray column</u> (<u>dorsal horn</u>)<br><br>* <u>Lateral gray column</u> (<u>lateral horn</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Contains cell bodies, <u>dendrites</u>, and <u>proximal</u> <u>axons</u> of <u>neurons</u><br><br>* For the function of each horn, see <u>anterior horn</u>, <u>dorsal horn</u>, and <u>lateral horn</u> in this table.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Centrally located, butterfly-like shape<br><br>* Surrounds the <u>central canal</u><br><br>* Gray commissure crosses the midline.<br><br><br> |
| Anterior horn | <br><br>* Contains cell bodies of motor <u>neurons</u><br><br>* Alpha motor neurons: lower motor neurons (<u>LMN</u>) whose <u>axons</u> extend into the periphery and innervate <u>extrafusal fibers</u> of <u>skeletal muscle</u><br><br>* Gamma motor neurons: innervate the <u>intrafusal fibers</u> of <u>muscle spindles</u><br><br>* Renshaw cells: inhibitory interneurons in the <u>anterior horn</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Alpha motor neurons</u> induce the contraction of <u>skeletal muscle</u>.<br><br>* <u>Gamma motor neurons</u> increase the stretch <u>sensitivity</u> of <u>muscle spindles</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Contains Rexed laminae VIII–IX<br><br>* Organized somatotopically<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> motor <u>neurons</u> innervate <u>proximal</u> musculature (e.g., the trunk and shoulders).<br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> motor <u>neurons</u> innervate <u>distal</u> musculature (e.g., the hands and feet).<br><br>* Motor <u>neurons</u> that innervate flexors are located dorsally and those that innervate extensors are located ventrally.<br><br><br> |
| Dorsal horn | <br>* Cell bodies of second-order sensory <u>neurons</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Transports sensory stimuli to the <u>brain stem</u>, <u>cerebral cortex</u>, or <u>cerebellum</u><br><br>* Involved in <u>spinal reflexes</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Contains <u>Rexed laminae</u> I–VI<br><br>* Marginal <u>nucleus</u> (lamina I)<br><br>* Substantia gelatinosa of Rolando (lamina II)<br><br>* <u>Nucleus</u> proprius (laminae III, IV)<br><br>* Spinal lamina V<br><br>* Spinal lamina VI<br><br> |
| Lateral horn | <br><br>* Extends from T1–L2<br><br>* <u>Clarke nucleus</u> (<u>posterior thoracic nucleus</u>) at T1–L3<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Contains <u>preganglionic</u> cell bodies of <u>sympathetic</u> <u>neurons</u><br><br>* Clarke nucleus: relays unconscious proprioception (unconscious perception of relative position and movement of the body) to the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Contains <u>Rexed lamina</u> VII<br><br> |
| Spinal nerves | <br><br>* Composed of <u>ventral</u> and <u>dorsal</u> <u>nerve roots</u> and rami<br><br>* 8 cervical <u>spinal nerves</u> (C1–C8)<br><br>* 12 thoracic <u>spinal nerves</u> (T1–T12)<br><br>* 5 lumbar <u>spinal nerves</u> (L1–L5)<br><br>* 5 sacral <u>spinal nerves</u> (<u>S1</u>–S5)<br><br>* 1 coccygeal <u>spinal nerve</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Transport autonomic, motor, and sensory signals between the spinal cord and the body<br><br> | <br>* There are 31 pairs of <u>spinal nerves</u>.<br><br> |
| Nerve roots | <br><br>* Exit the <u>spinal canal</u> via the <u>intervertebral foramina</u><br><br>* Cervical roots exit the canal above the <u>vertebra</u> that corresponds to the segment of the root (e.g., C8 <u>spinal nerve</u> exits above T1).<br><br>* Thoracic, lumbar, and sacral <u>nerve roots</u> exit below the corresponding <u>vertebra</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> roots carry motor (efferent) fibers that control skeletal and <u>smooth muscle</u>.<br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> roots carry sensor (afferent) fibers that transmit somatosensory information.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Disk herniation</u> is the most common cause of damage to the <u>spinal nerve</u> roots.<br><br> |
| Dorsal root ganglia | <br><br>* Present on every <u>dorsal</u> <u>nerve root</u><br><br>* Located in the <u>intervertebral foramina</u> outside the <u>vertebral column</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Carry sensory (afferent) fibers<br><br> | <br><br>* Develops from <u>neural crest cells</u><br><br>* Contains pseudo-unipolar neurons: sensory <u>neurons</u> in the <u>peripheral nervous system</u> containing an <u>axon</u> that splits into two branches<br><br><br> |
| Ventral rami | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> part of the <u>spinal nerve</u><br><br>* Branch from <u>spinal nerves</u> after leaving the <u>intervertebral foramen</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Innervate the <u>skin</u> and <u>skeletal muscle</u> of the anterolateral trunk and limbs<br><br> | <br>* Mixed nerves (relay both sensory and motor information)<br><br> |
| Dorsal rami | <br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> part of the <u>spinal nerve</u><br><br>* Branch from <u>spinal nerve</u> after leaving the <u>intervertebral foramen</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Innervate:<br><br>* <u>Skin</u> of the back and <u>dorsal</u> neck<br><br>* Deep <u>muscles of the back</u> (e.g., <u>erector spinae</u>)<br><br>* The <u>posterior</u> <u>vertebrae</u> and <u>facet joints</u><br><br>* <u>Superficial</u> <u>ligamenta flava</u><br><br> | <br>* Mixed nerves (relay both sensory and motor information)<br><br> |
| Cervical region | <br>* Cervical enlargement at C5–T1 level<br><br> | <br>* Forms the <u>brachial plexus</u>, which innervates the upper limb<br><br> | <br><br>* Large <u>anterior horn</u><br><br>* No <u>lateral horn</u><br><br>* Both <u>dorsal columns</u> are present.<br><br><br> |
| Thoracic region | <br>* Consists of 12 spinal segments (T1–T12); no enlargement at this level<br><br> | <br>* Origin of the intercostal nerves, which innervate: <br><br>* Thoracic wall<br><br>* <u>Parietal pleura</u> of the <u>lungs</u><br><br>* Abdominal wall<br><br>* <u>Peritoneum</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Small <u>anterior horn</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral horns</u> are present.<br><br>* <u>Dorsal columns</u> vary.<br><br><br> |
| Lumbar region | <br>* Lumbar enlargement at L2–<u>S3</u> level<br><br> | <br>* Forms lumbar and sacral plexuses, which innervate the lower limbs<br><br> | <br><br>* Large <u>anterior horn</u><br><br>* No <u>lateral horn</u><br><br>* One <u>dorsal column</u> is present.<br><br><br> |
| Conus medullaris | <br><br>* <u>Caudal</u> end of the spinal cord consisting of upper and <u>lower motor neurons</u><br><br>* Origin of <u>S2</u>–S5 <u>spinal nerves</u><br><br>* Ends at the L2 <u>vertebral</u> level (in adults)<br><br><br> | <br>* Innervates lower extremities, bowel, and <u>bladder</u><br><br> | <br>* Tapered terminal end of spinal cord; directly attached to <u>filum terminale</u><br><br> |
| Cauda equina | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> and <u>dorsal</u> <u>nerve roots</u> of <u>spinal nerves</u> (L2–Co1)<br><br>* Lumbar<br><br>* Sacral<br><br>* Coccygeal<br><br> | <br><br>* Innervates the lower limb, <u>perineum</u>, and <u>pelvic</u> organs<br><br>* Innervates the internal and <u>external anal sphincter</u><br><br>* Provides <u>parasympathetic</u> innervation to the <u>bladder</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Bundle of tapered <u>nerve roots</u> resembles a horse's tail<br><br> |
| Filum terminale | <br>* Thin extension of <u>pia mater</u><br><br> | <br>* Attaches the bottom of the spinal cord to the <u>vertebral column</u><br><br> | <br>* Slender, string-like appearance<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Renshaw cells</u> are inhibitory interneurons that secrete <u>glycine</u>. These are the <u>neurons</u> targeted by <u>Clostridium tetani</u> toxin.

### Blood supply of the spinal cord




* <u>Vertebral arteries</u>

* Main source of blood supply to the spinal cord

* Arise from the <u>subclavian artery</u>

* Branches

* Anterior spinal artery 

* Supplies the <u>anterior</u> two-thirds of the spinal cord and the lower medulla at the midline

* Sits in the <u>anterior</u> median <u>fissure</u> of the spinal cord

* Has penetrating and circumferential branches

* Posterior spinal arteries supply the <u>posterior</u> part of the spinal cord bilaterally.

* Arterial vasocorona: <u>anastomosis</u> between spinal <u>arteries</u>

* Segmental spinal <u>arteries</u>

* Enter the <u>vertebral canal</u> via <u>intervertebral foramina</u> at every level

* Arise from various <u>arteries</u> depending on anatomic location  

* Neck: <u>vertebral</u> and deep cervical <u>arteries</u>

* Thorax: <u>posterior intercostal arteries</u>

* Abdomen: <u>lumbar arteries</u>

* Branch to <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> radicular <u>arteries</u> in the <u>intervertebral foramen</u> and supply <u>nerve roots</u> and the spinal cord
* Give rise to the great anterior radiculomedullary artery (<u>artery of Adamkiewicz</u>) in the lower thoracic region

* <u>Anastomoses</u> with the <u>anterior spinal artery</u>

* Supplies the spinal cord from T8 and below

* <u>Vertebral</u> <u>veins</u>: See the <u>vertebral column</u> article for more information on the venous system of the spinal cord.





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>great anterior radiculomedullary artery</u> (<u>artery of Adamkiewicz</u>) is the dominant <u>artery</u> supplying the thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord.

## Spinal cord tracts

The spinal cord contains ascending and descending tracts. The primary ascending tracts use three <u>neurons</u> to relay peripheral sensory information to the <u>brain</u>. In contrast, the descending tracts transmit motor impulses from the <u>cerebral cortex</u> throughout the body. For more information on lesions of the <u>spinal cord tracts</u> see the <u>incomplete spinal cord syndromes</u> article.




### Ascending (sensory) tracts [[1]](/library/DPY1S6)[[2]](/library/tMbXq8)




| Tract | Function | First-order <u>neuron</u> | <u>Synapses</u> | Second-order <u>neuron</u> | Trajectory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conscious sensation |  |  |  |  |  |
| Spinothalamic tract | <br><br>* Pressure sensation (<u>anterior</u>)<br><br>* Protopathic sensation<br><br>* Temperature (<u>lateral</u>)<br><br>* <u>Pain</u> (<u>lateral</u>)<br><br>* Crude touch (<u>anterior</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Sensory nerve fibers (<u>Aδ fibers</u> and <u>C fibers</u>) have pseudounipolar cell bodies in the <u>dorsal root ganglion</u>.<br><br>* <u>Axon</u> enters the spinal cord and ascends or descends several segments in the posterolateral tract (<u>Lissauer tract</u>).<br><br>* Located at tips of <u>dorsal horns</u><br><br>* Carries ascending sensory fibers one to two levels above before synapsing in the <u>dorsal horn</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> spinal cord in the substantia gelatinosa or <u>nucleus</u> proprius one to two segments below or above the 1<sup>st</sup><u>neuron</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Axon</u> <u>decussates</u> within the <u>anterior</u> white commissure and then ascends contralaterally.<br><br>* In the <u>lateral</u> <u>spinothalamic tract</u>, cervical segments are <u>medial</u> and sacral segments are <u>lateral</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* To the 3<sup>rd</sup><u>neuron</u> in the <u>ventral posterolateral nucleus</u> of the <u>thalamus</u> → <u>somatosensory cortex</u><br><br> |
| Dorsal column | <br><br>* <u>Proprioception</u><br><br>* Epicritic sensation: <u>fine touch</u>, vibration, pressure sensation<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Sensory nerve fibers have a pseudounipolar cell body in the <u>dorsal root ganglion</u>.<br><br>* <u>Axon</u> enters the spinal cord and ascends ipsilaterally<br><br>* <u>Gracile fasciculus</u> (sensation from lower limbs, T6 and below): located medially<br><br>* <u>Cuneate fasciculus</u> (sensation from upper limbs, T5 and above): located laterally<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> <u>medulla oblongata</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Axon</u> <u>decussates</u> to the <u>contralateral</u> side within the medulla.<br><br>* Ascends contralaterally in the <u>medial lemniscus</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Unconscious sensation [[3]](/library/vPYAg6)<br> |  |  |  |  |  |
| Spinocerebellar tract | <br>* <u>Proprioception</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Sensory nerve fibers<br><br>* Cell body in the <u>dorsal root ganglion</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> <u>posterior horn</u> of the spinal cord<br><br> | <br>* <u>Axons</u> arising from the <u>posterior horn</u> of the spinal cord to the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebellum</u> (via inferior and <u>superior cerebellar peduncles</u>)<br><br> |
| Spinoolivary tract | <br>* <u>Proprioception</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Axons</u> arising from the <u>posterior horn</u> of the spinal cord to the olivary <u>nuclei</u> of the medulla<br><br> | <br>* Third-order <u>neurons</u> to the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br> |  |  |

### Descending (motor) tracts [[1]](/library/DPY1S6)[[2]](/library/tMbXq8)




| Tract | Function | First-order <u>neuron</u> | <u>Synapses</u> | Second-order <u>neuron</u> | Trajectory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Corticospinal tract<br>(part of the pyramidal tract) [[4]](/library/wPYhS6)<br> | <br>* Voluntary movement of the <u>contralateral</u> side<br><br> | <br><br>* Upper motor neuron<br><br>* Cell body in the motor cortex (precentral <u>gyrus</u>)<br><br>* Descends ipsilaterally via the <u>internal capsule</u> (<u>posterior</u> limb)<br><br>* Lateral corticospinal tract (∼ 80% of fibers)<br><br>* Crosses in the <u>caudal</u> medulla (<u>pyramidal decussation</u>)<br><br>* Descends in the spinal cord contralaterally<br><br>* Cervical segments are <u>medial</u> and sacral segments are <u>lateral</u>.<br><br>* Anterior corticospinal tract (∼ 20% of fibers): Crosses at the same level of the <u>spine</u> as it innervates (not at the level of the <u>medulla oblongata</u>).<br><br><br> | <br>* Anterior horn cells: motor <u>neurons</u> in the <u>anterior gray column</u> of the spinal cord<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lower motor neurons</u> of the upper or lower limbs<br><br> | <br>* To the <u>neuromuscular junction</u> (NMJ) of respective muscles<br><br> |
| Extrapyramidal tracts | <br>* Regulate the action of motor <u>neurons</u><br><br>* Involuntary movement (e.g., equilibratory reflexes, visual and auditory reflexes)<br><br>* Muscle tone<br><br>* Musculature responsible for facial expressions<br><br> | <br>* Multiple projections and pathways<br><br>* Rubrospinal pathway<br><br>* <u>Reticulospinal tract</u><br><br>* <u>Vestibulospinal tract</u><br><br>* <u>Tectospinal tract</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Anterior horn cells</u> of the spinal cord<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lower motor neurons</u><br><br> | <br>* Varies depending on the tract<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Legs are represented Laterally in the Lateral spinothalamic and Lateral <u>corticospinal tract</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Remember that fasciculus graciLis carries sensory information from the Lower limbs, and fasciculus cUneatus transmits information from the Upper limbs.

## Spinal cord reflexes

### Reflex innervation of <u>skeletal muscles</u> [[1]](/library/DPY1S6)[[2]](/library/tMbXq8)[[4]](/library/wPYhS6)




* Definition: Reflexes are involuntary, consistent reactions to specific stimuli.

* Reflex arc

* Reflex arc consists of

* Somatosensory <u>receptors</u> (e.g., <u>muscle spindles</u>, <u>Golgi tendon organs</u>)

* Afferent nerve fibers (e.g., <u>type Ia fibers</u> and <u>type II fibers</u>)

* Integrating center (e.g., the spinal cord in <u>spinal reflexes</u>)

* Efferent nerve fibers (e.g., <u>axons</u> of <u>alpha motor neurons</u>)

* Effector organs (mostly muscles)

* The reflex arc of <u>spinal reflexes</u> does not involve the <u>brain</u> or <u>brainstem</u>. However, <u>upper motor neurons</u> may modify the intensity of the reflex response. See <u>upper motor neuron damage</u> for more information.





### Muscle <u>proprioceptors</u>




|  | Muscle spindle | Golgi tendon organ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | <br>* <u>Intrafusal muscle fibers</u> (modified <u>skeletal muscle</u> fibers) and nerve fibers surrounded by a capsule<br><br> | <br>* <u>Collagen</u> strands and nerve fibers surrounded by a capsule<br><br> |
| Location | <br>* Within <u>skeletal muscle</u>; parallel to <u>extrafusal muscle fibers</u><br><br> | <br>* Within <u>tendons</u> of <u>skeletal muscle</u><br><br> |
| Perception | <br>* Muscle length and change of muscle length (e.g., muscle stretching)<br><br> | <br>* Muscle tension and muscle force<br><br> |
| Reflex arc | <br>* Myotatic stretch reflex  <br><br>* Alteration of muscle length activates <u>muscle spindles</u><br><br>* Afferent signals travel via <u>type Ia fibers</u> and <u>type II fibers</u> and the <u>dorsal root ganglion</u> to the spinal cord.<br><br>* Simultaneous activation of:<br><br>* <u>Alpha motor neurons</u> (<u>LMNs</u>) that innervate the <u>agonist</u> muscle (monosynaptic)<br><br>* Inhibitory interneurons that inhibit the <u>alpha motor neurons</u> of the <u>antagonist</u> muscle (disynaptic)<br><br>* See <u>tendon reflexes</u> for more information.<br><br> | <br>* Inverse myotatic stretch reflex  <br><br>* Tension of the muscle activates <u>Golgi tendon organs</u>.<br><br>* Afferent signals travel via <u>type Ib sensory fibers</u> and the <u>dorsal root ganglion</u> to the spinal cord.<br><br>* Activation of inhibitory interneurons that inhibit the <u>alpha motor neurons</u> of the <u>agonist</u> muscle (disynaptic)<br><br>* Relaxation of the <u>agonist</u> muscle (prevents exhaustive tension)<br><br> |
| Purpose | <br>* Causes stretched muscle to contract<br><br> | <br><br>* Controls <u>tendon</u> tension of activated muscle<br><br>* Causes muscle relaxation of <u>agonist</u> muscle before <u>tendon</u> damage occurs<br><br><br> |
| Example | <br>* Tapping of reflex hammer on <u>tendon</u><br><br> | <br>* Sudden relaxation when a weightlifter uses extremely heavy weights<br><br> |

### Clinically important reflexes




Deep <u>tendon</u> (stretch) reflexes are <u>ipsilateral</u> and only require one <u>synapse</u> (monosynaptic).




* Afferent limb: a sensory <u>neuron</u> from <u>muscle spindles</u> that travels to the spinal cord

* Efferent limb: a <u>lower motor neuron</u> that travels from the spinal cord to the <u>neuromuscular junction</u>





| Reflex | Muscle tested | Spinal level |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Biceps reflex</u> | <u>Biceps</u> | C5–C6 |
| <u>Brachioradialis reflex</u> | <u>Brachioradialis</u> | C5–C6 |
| <u>Triceps reflex</u> | <u>Triceps</u> | C7–C8 |
| <u>Knee reflex</u> (patellar) | <u>Quadriceps</u> | L3–L4 |
| <u>Ankle reflex</u> (Achilles) | <u>Gastrocnemius</u> | <u>S1</u>–<u>S2</u> |
| <u>Cremasteric reflex</u> | Cremaster | L1–L2 |
| <u>Anal wink</u> reflex | <u>External anal sphincter</u> | <u>S3</u>–S5 |





* See <u>tendon reflexes</u> for more information.

* See sensory <u>receptors</u> of the <u>skin</u> for more details on <u>mechanoreceptors</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> Think of this poem to remember which <u>nerve roots</u> correspond to which reflexes:
> <u>S1</u>–<u>S2</u>
> Buckle my shoe (<u>ankle reflex</u>),
> L2–L4
> Kick the door (<u>knee reflex</u>),
> C5–C6
> Pick up sticks (<u>biceps</u> and <u>brachioradialis reflexes</u>),
> C7–C8
> Lay them straight (<u>triceps reflex</u>),
> L1–L2
> <u>Testicle</u> move (<u>cremasteric reflex</u>),
> <u>S3</u>–S5
> Winking drive (<u>anal wink</u> reflex).

## Dermatomes

<u>Dermatomes</u> are areas of cutaneous innervation that are supplied by a single <u>spinal nerve</u> or cord level (with the exception of <u>cranial nerves</u> V1–3). While there is some overlap in the general distribution of <u>dermatomes</u>, each individual spinal cord level supplies a distinct zone of <u>skin</u>. Testing touch or sensory perception in these areas can be used to localize lesions of the spinal cord to a specific cord level or <u>spinal nerve</u>. [[2]](/library/tMbXq8)[[5]](/library/iRYJ5K)




### Head <u>dermatomes</u>




| <u>Dermatome</u> | Distribution |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Cranial nerve V1</u> | <br><br>* Ophthalmic branch of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u><br><br>* Upper face<br><br>* Dorsum of the nose<br><br>* <u>Orbit</u> (including <u>conjunctiva</u> and <u>cornea</u>)<br><br>* Forehead<br><br>* Upper eyelids<br><br><br> |
| <u>Cranial nerve V2</u> | <br><br>* <u>Maxillary branch</u> of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u><br><br>* Midface<br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> nose<br><br>* Anteroinferior part of the <u>nasal septum</u><br><br>* Upper lip and cheeks<br><br>* Lower eyelids<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> region of the temple (<u>anterior</u> to <u>the ear</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Cranial nerve V3</u> | <br><br>* Mandibular branch of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u><br><br>* Lower face<br><br>* <u>External auditory meatus</u> (including the <u>tympanic membrane</u>)<br><br>* Preauricular area of external <u>ear</u> and tragus<br><br>* Lower lip and chin<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> region of the temple (<u>posterior</u> to <u>the ear</u>)<br><br>* Chin area of the <u>mandible</u><br><br>* <u>Temporomandibular joint</u><br><br><br> |
| C1–C4 | <br>* From the <u>cervical plexus</u> <br><br>* Angle of the <u>mandible</u><br><br>* External <u>ear</u> (<u>posterior</u> part)<br><br>* Inframandibular region (<u>submandibular triangle</u>)<br><br>* Occipital protuberance<br><br> |

| <u>Dermatome</u> | Distribution |
| --- | --- |
| C2 | <u>Posterior</u> half of <u>skull</u> |
| C3 | Upper neck, directly inferior to the <u>mandible</u><br> |
| C4 | Above the <u>clavicle</u>, including upper shoulders and <u>trapezius</u><br> |
| C5 | Below the <u>clavicle</u>, including lower shoulders bilaterally and <u>medial</u> <u>biceps</u><br> |
| C6 | <u>Lateral</u> aspect of forearms and thumbs |
| C7 | Middle <u>triceps</u> and mid-palm, including index and middle fingers<br> |
| C8 | <br><u>Medial</u> <u>triceps</u> and <u>medial</u> palm, including ring and small fingers<br> |
| T4 | Level of the <u>nipples</u> |
| T7 | <u>Xiphoid process</u> |

### <u>Referred pain</u> in <u>dermatomes</u>




<u>Referred pain</u> is the perception of sensory information in a location that differs from the actual site of the stimulus. The <u>pain</u> is sensed from a particular spinal cord level but the <u>CNS</u> interprets this <u>pain</u> as coming from another location that is innervated by the same spinal cord level.




| Spinal cord level | Organ | Area of <u>referred pain</u> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C3–C5 | <u>Diaphragm</u> via <u>phrenic nerve</u> | Shoulder |
| T10 | <br><u>Appendix</u> via <u>greater splanchnic nerve</u><br> | Umbilical region |
| T1–T4 | <u>Heart</u> | Upper thorax and left arm |
| T5–T9 | <br><u>Foregut</u> (organs supplied by the <u>celiac trunk</u>) | Lower thorax and epigastrium |
| T10–T12 | <br><u>Midgut</u> (organs supplied by the <u>superior mesenteric artery</u>) | Umbilical region |
| L1–L2 | <br><u>Hindgut</u> (organs supplied by the <u>inferior mesenteric artery</u>) | Hypogastrium and groin |
| T12 | <u>Kidneys</u> and <u>ureters</u> | <u>Lateral</u> flanks and pubic region |





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the segments that innervate the <u>diaphragm</u>, think of “C3–C5 keep the <u>diaphragm</u> alive.”

## Embryology of the spinal cord

<u>Neurulation</u> begins during the third week of <u>gestation</u>, during which the <u>neural plate</u> folds over at the midline and fuses to form the <u>neural tube</u>. The <u>neural tube</u> then forms both the spinal cord and <u>brain</u>.




### <u>Neurulation</u> derivatives




| Structure | Characteristics | Derivatives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Notochord</u> | <br>* Induces overlying <u>ectoderm</u> to differentiate into the <u>neuroectoderm</u> and form the <u>neural plate</u> (occurs on 18<sup>th</sup> day of <u>gestation</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Nucleus pulposus</u> of the intervertebral disk<br><br> |
| <u>Neural plate</u> | <br><br>* Located on the <u>dorsal</u> portion of the trilaminar germ disk<br><br>* Precursor structure for the process of <u>neurulation</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Neural tube</u><br><br> |
| Neural folds | <br><br>* Grow dorsally toward the midline; fuse together to form the <u>neural tube</u><br><br>* Occurs at the end of the 3<sup>rd</sup> week (21<sup>st</sup> day) of <u>gestation</u><br><br>* Located on the free edges of the <u>neural plate</u> bilaterally during the elongation and folding process<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Neural crest cells</u><br><br> |
| <u>Neural crest cells</u> | <br><br>* Group of cells that arises from neural folds<br><br>* After the neural folds fuse and form the roof of the <u>neural tube</u>, <u>neural crest cells</u> transition from <u>epithelial</u> to <u>mesenchymal</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Dorsal root ganglia</u><br><br>* Autonomic <u>ganglia</u><br><br>* <u>Schwann cells</u><br><br>* <u>Adrenal medulla</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Neural tube</u> | <br><br>* Consists of two plates<br><br>* Alar plate (<u>dorsal</u>) regulated by <u>proteins</u> of the <u>TGF-β</u> family (e.g., <u>bone morphogenetic protein</u>)<br><br>* <u>Basal plate</u> (<u>ventral</u>) regulated by <u>sonic hedgehog</u> protein<br><br>* Formed by the fusion of neural folds, deepening of the neural groove, and elongation of the <u>neural plate</u><br><br>* Has 3 primary <u>vesicles</u>, which develop into 5 <u>vesicles</u><br><br>* Has <u>rostral</u> and <u>caudal</u> openings (<u>neuropores</u>)<br><br>* Rostral neuropore (<u>anterior</u>): closes by the 26<sup>th</sup> day of <u>embryonic development</u><br><br>* Caudal neuropore (<u>posterior</u>): closes by the 28<sup>th</sup> day of <u>embryonic development</u><br><br>* Failure of the <u>neural tube</u> to completely close results in <u>neural tube defects</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* Gives rise to the <u>brain</u> and the spinal cord<br><br>* Alar plate gives rise to sensory <u>neurons</u>.<br><br>* <u>Basal plate</u> gives rise to motor <u>neurons</u>.<br><br> |





See also “<u>Neurulation</u>” in <u>embryogenesis</u> for more information.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>rostral neuropore</u> closes by day 26, the <u>caudal neuropore</u> closes by day 28. The failure of <u>neuropores</u> to completely close causes <u>neural tube defects</u> (e.g., <u>spina bifida</u>).

## Clinical significance

### <u>Complete spinal cord injuries</u>



* <u>Spinal shock</u>




### <u>Incomplete spinal cord injuries</u>




* <u>Central cord syndrome</u>

* <u>Anterior cord syndrome</u>

* <u>Posterior cord syndrome</u>

* <u>Brown-Séquard syndrome</u>





### Other spinal cord pathologies




* <u>Epidural hematoma</u>

* <u>Multiple sclerosis</u>

* <u>Degenerative disk disease</u>

* <u>Syringomyelia</u>

* <u>Myelopathy</u>

* <u>Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</u>

* <u>Subacute combined degeneration</u>

* <u>Cauda equina syndrome</u>

* <u>Conus medullaris syndrome</u>

* <u>Spina bifida</u>

* <u>Anterior spinal artery syndrome</u>

* Posterior spinal artery syndrome: loss of function of the cord that is supplied by the <u>posterior spinal arteries</u>, namely the <u>posterior</u> (<u>dorsal</u>) columns, resulting in loss of <u>proprioception</u> and vibratory sensation at and below the level of the injury

* <u>Tabes dorsalis</u>

* <u>Hereditary spastic paraplegia</u>

* <u>Spinal muscular atrophy</u>

* <u>Poliomyelitis</u>





### Spinal arteriovenous malformation [[6]](/library/1OX2ry)




* Definition: congenital <u>malformation</u> of spinal <u>blood vessels</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: usually presents in younger patients

* Pathophysiology: abnormal arteriovenous connections of spinal <u>arteries</u> to <u>veins</u> within the <u>dura</u> (<u>intramedullary</u>, mostly thoracic or lumbar) → arterialization of spinal <u>veins</u> → congestive <u>myelopathy</u> because of venous <u>hypertension</u>, stasis, and multi-segmental <u>spinal cord lesions</u> → <u>mass effect</u> and/or <u>ischemia</u> and/or hemorrhage into the cord

* Clinical features 

* Features of <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u> (e.g., <u>headache</u>, <u>photophobia</u>)

* Features of <u>intraparenchymal hemorrhage</u> (e.g., localized <u>pain</u>, distinct level of <u>paresthesia</u> and <u>paraplegia</u>, urinary and <u>fecal incontinence</u>)

* <u>Mass effect</u> of <u>arteriovenous malformations</u> (e.g., <u>spinal cord compression</u>)

* Diagnostics

* <u>MRI</u>: cluster of low-intensity signal foci

* Spinal <u>digital subtraction angiography</u> (<u>DSA</u>)

* Treatment: possibly endovascular embolization/occlusion or surgical resection (depends on type and localization) [[7]](/library/WOXPry)

* Complications: <u>tetraplegia</u> with motor and sensory loss
